data.full_text:
Abstract This retrospective diagnostic accuracy study evaluated the performance of an artificial intelligence (AI) platform (Diagnocat) in assessing endodontic treatment features via panoramic (PAN) and cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) images from 163 patients. Two experienced observers (a radiologist and a dentist) provided consensus readings on the CBCT images, which served as the reference standard. Because the platform applies modality-specific processing pipelines, analyses were conducted and reported separately for CBCT and PAN. The AI analyzed five treatment variables—adequate obturation, adequate density, overfilling, voids in filling, and short filling—and its performance was compared against the reference standard for both the PAN and the CBCT. Diagnostic accuracy, precision, recall (sensitivity), and F1-scores were calculated. Diagnocat exhibited excellent diagnostic performance on CBCT images, achieving overall accuracy above 94% and perfect (100%) sensitivity for overfilling. On PAN benchmarked against the CBCT reference, performance was lower (accuracies 68.25–84.66%), with limited precision and F1-scores for adequate obturation and adequate density, while sensitivity remained comparatively high for voids and short fillings. These results demonstrate modality-dependent platform performance under the studied acquisition protocols and reference standard.

Introduction According to the most recent systematic review and meta-analysis by Tibúrcio-Machado et al.., apical periodontitis—closely associated with infection of the root canal system—affects approximately 52% of the global adult population1. Successful endodontic treatment relies on thorough disinfection of the root canal system and prevention of reinfection through proper instrumentation, irrigation, and obturation2. Radiographic evaluation is a critical component of assessing the success of endodontic treatments. The key factors indicating treatment success are the absence of periapical radiolucency and the presence of well-sealed root canal filling2. The success of endodontic treatment is largely influenced by the quality of the root canal filling, with deficiencies in its extent and continuity negatively affecting the treatment outcome3. The lack of pathologic radiolucency in follow-up radiographs is a crucial sign of successful treatment4. For decades, dentists have relied on two-dimensional (2D) imaging, such as periapical radiographs (PRs) and panoramic radiographs (PAN)2. Radiographic imaging plays a crucial role in both dental treatment planning and outcome assessment5,6. PAN images are often used for initial screening because they provide a comprehensive overview of the entire jaw, teeth, and surrounding structures. As a result, PAN is frequently adopted as the initial imaging approach in dental settings and remains one of the most prescribed examinations7. However, both PAN images and the more targeted PRs suffer from significant limitations because they flatten three-dimensional (3D) anatomy into a 2D image. This can create “anatomic noise” from superimposed structures and geometric distortions, which may hide underlying problems such as bone loss, complex canal systems, or subtle treatment flaws8,9. Both PRs and PAN images provide only a two-dimensional representation (2D) of inherently three-dimensional (3D) anatomical structures, leading to significant limitations, such as the superimposition of the overlying anatomy (anatomic noise) and geometric distortion, which can obscure pathology or complex canal morphology10,11,12. Consequently, periapical lesions may only become apparent after substantial bone loss, and subtle anatomical features or treatment deficiencies can be missed. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) has emerged as a valuable adjunct, offering cross-sectional, three-dimensional visualization of the teeth and surrounding tissues. This technology overcomes many limitations of 2D imaging, demonstrating greater accuracy and sensitivity in detecting periapical lesions, identifying missed canals, evaluating the quality of root canal fillings, and assessing complex anatomical relationships13,14. The advantages of CBCT in endodontics have been recognized by practicing clinicians, leading to widespread adoption of this technology in endodontic practice15. Artificial intelligence (AI), especially convolutional neural networks (CNNs), is being increasingly widely applied in medicine, particularly in radiology and computer-aided diagnosis (CAD). Studies have already demonstrated that CNNs can be used in dental radiology and in evaluating endodontic treatment outcomes16,17,18,19,20. With increasing radiological exam volumes and heavier practitioner workloads, various commercially available AI solutions have been developed to support diagnostic processes. One such tool is Diagnocat (Diagnocat Ltd., San Francisco, CA, USA), which employs CNNs trained on more than 35,000 dental radiographs to increase diagnostic accuracy. Some studies have shown that Diagnocat can identify various dental pathologies (caries, periapical lesions, impacted teeth, etc.) and anatomical landmarks with a high level of accuracy21,22. Preliminary studies also indicated that this program might be useful in endodontic treatment evaluation23,24. However, these studies have several limitations, including small sample sizes and separate evaluations of PAN and CBCT examinations. Additionally, the program demonstrated variable performance, with low accuracy in detecting certain features of endodontic fillings on PAN images23. Prior studies evaluating this platform have typically assessed PAN and CBCT separately and often in smaller cohorts, with variable performance reported for certain endodontic features on PAN. Importantly, PAN and CBCT are distinct imaging modalities with different information content and artefact profiles, and commercial platforms commonly deploy modality-specific processing pipelines. Therefore, in the present work we evaluate and report the platform’s end-to-end diagnostic performance separately on PAN and on CBCT in the same patient cohort, using a single common reference standard. The aim of present study was to quantify the diagnostic agreement of the AI platform’s outputs with a CBCT reader consensus reference for key post-endodontic radiographic features when applied to (i) CBCT examinations and (ii) PAN examinations acquired from the same patients. As a secondary objective, we describe how AI performance on PAN compares with human PAN assessment when both are benchmarked against the CBCT consensus reference. Results Population The final study group consisted of 163 patients, including 112 females (68.71%) and 51 males (31.29%). The mean age of the participants was 31.29 ± 14.2 years, with a median age of 30 years and a range of 8–65 years. In total, the patient sample presented 4,646 teeth, of which 189 had received endodontic treatment. No adverse events related to imaging were reported during the period in which the examinations used in this study were conducted at the dental center. The demographic characteristics of the participants in the final study group are detailed in Table 1. Table 1 The baseline demographic of the final study group. Full size table Study power analysis A power analysis was conducted to justify the sample size, assuming a desired power of 80% and a confidence level of 95%. The sample size was estimated via the Buderer method, with calculations based on the observed sensitivity, specificity, and feature prevalence from the dataset25. With 189 endodontically treated teeth, the study sample was sufficient to estimate diagnostic sensitivity and specificity, with a precision of ± 5% points for most of the analyzed parameters across all comparisons. For example, in the AI PAN vs. Reader CBCT comparison, the required sample sizes for ± 5 p.p. precision ranged from 50 for “Overfilling” to 195 for “Adequate obturation,” demonstrating the adequacy of our sample size for almost all assessed features. For features with low prevalence (e.g., “adequate obturation” on PAN), the sample size required to guarantee ± 5 p.p. precision may be slightly larger than our cohort. Estimates for these endpoints should be interpreted with appropriate caution and verified in larger multicenter datasets. For the AI CBCT vs. Reader CBCT analysis, the required sample sizes for this level of precision were well below our included number, such as 61 for “adequate obturation” and 38 for “voids in filling”. Diagnostic accuracy The diagnostic performance of the AI tool and the PAN-based reader assessment was evaluated against the reference standard (reader CBCT consensus) and in direct comparison (AI PAN vs. Reader PAN). The metrics of accuracy, precision, sensitivity (recall), and F1 score were calculated for five key features of endodontic fillings. There were no indeterminate results, as the readers unanimously reached a consensus on the diagnoses. Furthermore, any feature with a probability of occurrence exceeding 50% was deemed positive by the AI platform. The number of endodontically treated teeth diagnosed by the AI tool and by human readers was the same across both the PAN and the CBCT reader analyses, as was the case for the AI CBCT analysis (n = 189). However, the total number of positive diagnoses generated by the AI in the PAN analyses was greater, reaching 194. All five additional teeth identified by the AI platform in the PAN analysis were misdiagnosed. Sample false-positive diagnoses are shown in Fig. 1. The total number and enumeration of endodontically treated teeth were consistent in both the CBCT analyses and Readers’ consensus PAN analysis. Fig. 1 Full size image Sample false positive- and false negative diagnoses of AI platform on the presence of endodontic material in PAN analysis. (A) False positive, tooth 26, woman 19 years of age. (B) Tooth 27, filling in tooth 26 misdiagnosed as filling in tooth 27, woman 36 years of age. (C) Tooth 36, false positive diagnosis, woman 47 years of age. (D) Tooth 12, false negative diagnosis, woman 37 years of age. (E) Tooth 47, false positive diagnosis, man 35 years of age. AI performance on CBCT images (reference: reader CBCT) The AI demonstrated high diagnostic performance when analyzing CBCT images. For all the parameters, the accuracy was above 94%. The AI achieved perfect sensitivity (100.00%) for detecting “overfilling” and a high F1 score of 98.51% for “short filling”. The lowest performing metric was the precision for “adequate density” at 83.78%. The detailed results are presented in Table 2; Fig. 2. Table 2 Diagnostic performance of AI software in CBCT images analysis, with Reader CBCT as the reference standard. Full size table Fig. 2 Full size image Summary of diagnostic performance metrics of AI software in CBCT images analysis, with Reader CBCT as the reference standard (columns—mean values, bars—95% confidence intervals (CI)). AI and reader performance on PAN images (reference: reader CBCT) When analyzing PAN images against the CBCT reference, both the AI and the human reader showed a marked decrease in performance, particularly for assessing the quality of obturation. The AI accuracy decreased significantly, with values ranging from 68.25% for “adequate obturation” to 84.66% for “short filling”. The detection of “adequate density” proved most challenging for both the AI and the human reader, who achieved low precision (41.03% and 40.51%, respectively) and F1 scores (42.67% and 55.65%, respectively). The human reader generally achieved slightly higher accuracy than the AI on PAN images for most parameters, except for “short filling”. The performance metrics are summarized in Table 3; Fig. 3. Samples of false negative diagnoses of “Overfilling” are presented in Fig. 4. Table 3 Comparative diagnostic performance of AI PAN and Reader PAN, with Reader CBCT as the reference standard. Full size table Fig. 3 Full size image Comparison of diagnostic performance metrics of AI software and Readers’ consensus in PAN analyses, with Reader CBCT as the reference standard (columns—mean values, bars—95% confidence intervals (CI)). Fig. 4 Full size image Sample false negative diagnoses of AI platform in “Overfilling” assessment in both PAN and CBCT analysis. (A) Tooth 11, CBCT, woman 36 years of age. (B) Tooth 11, PAN, woman 37 years of age. (C) Tooth 15, PAN, woman 24 years of age (green arrow). (D) Tooth 26, CBCT, man 45 years of age. (E) Tooth 46, CBCT, man 45 years of age. (F) Tooth 44, PAN, woman 27 years of age. AI performance on PAN images (reference: reader PAN) To assess the AI’s performance specifically against human interpretation of the same 2D modality, the AI PAN results were compared directly with the Reader PAN findings. In this comparison, the AI showed high recall for most parameters, notably, 96.30% for “voids in filling” and 95.90% for “short filling”. However, its precision and accuracy for “adequate density” remained low (82.05% and 71.43%, respectively), with a correspondingly low recall of 40.51%. The detailed results are presented in Table 4; Fig. 5. Table 4 Diagnostic performance of AI on PAN images, with Reader PAN as the reference standard. Full size table Discussion The objective of this study was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of an AI tool in assessing the radiological features of endodontic treatment in PAN images and CBCT scans obtained from the same patients. The findings demonstrated that the AI platform achieved high diagnostic performance for CBCT analyses and acceptable PAN analyses. In particular, the AI tool exceeded 94% accuracy in evaluating all the endodontic features in the CBCT images. In contrast, accuracy in the PAN assessments was lower, with the lowest metrics observed in the obturation and density evaluations (68–77%). Furthermore, our analysis indicated that the performance of the AI tool and human readers in interpreting PAN images was comparable when measured against the CBCT reference standard. Our findings indicate that the analyzed AI platform may serve as a precise tool for CBCT assessment following endodontic treatment. AI is playing an increasingly significant role in modern dentistry, encompassing various fields such as orthodontics, surgery, conservative dentistry, and pediatric dentistry26,27,28,29. A recent review demonstrated numerous applications of AI algorithms in endodontics19,30. Numerous studies have demonstrated the utility of AI, particularly deep learning models such as convolutional neural networks (CNNs), for critical diagnostic tasks that are central to evaluating endodontic success. AI models have been effectively trained to detect radiolucent periapical lesions—a key indicator of treatment healing—across various imaging modalities, including panoramic and CBCT images17,31. These applications range from classification tasks that determine the presence or absence of a lesion to more advanced object detection and segmentation methods that identify and delineate the pathology32. Furthermore, research has moved beyond simple lesion detection to more direct prognostic applications, using AI to predict the outcome of root canal treatments by analyzing factors such as the quality of root fillings on radiographic images and other clinical data33,34. Other relevant AI applications that impact treatment outcomes include the detection of vertical root fractures and separated instruments, which are common causes of posttreatment failure35,36. This established body of work underscores the potential for AI to serve as a reliable tool in the nuanced task of evaluating and predicting endodontic treatment outcomes. PR remains the primary imaging modality for evaluating postendodontic treatment outcomes, despite persisting debate across guidelines concerning the necessity and schedule of follow-up37. However, the use of PR images is inherently associated with several challenges, including the superimposition of anatomical structures, geometric distortion, anatomical noise, and, ultimately, their two-dimensional nature38. Furthermore, low contrast and poorly defined tooth contours constitute additional factors that hinder the diagnostic process39. The same limitations also apply to PAN images. Furthermore, PAN images often provide insufficient resolution for capturing the fine details commonly required in endodontics. Consequently, it is a less preferred imaging modality among physicians, who typically opt for more suitable alternatives such as PR or CBCT2,6. Although the PAN provides a comprehensive view of the maxillofacial region, its diagnostic accuracy in detailed assessments is questionable. PAN is a reliable diagnostic modality for assessing the number of remaining teeth, the number of root-filled teeth and the DMFT score40. However, compared with intraoral periapical radiographs, PAN images have lower resolution, which can obscure critical details such as minor canal overfillings41. One study reported that PAN achieved a diagnostic accuracy of 71.3%, with 93.8% specificity but only 48.8% sensitivity for detecting endodontically treated apical periodontitis relative to CBCT9. These limitations contribute to interobserver variability and warrant caution when interpreting PAN findings. However, owing to their high versatility, PAN images remain an initial screening test in everyday dental practice. Multiple studies report that three-dimensional imaging may reveal post-treatment features that are less conspicuous on two-dimensional radiographs, particularly in complex anatomy or in the presence of superimposition and geometric distortion42,43. Lo Giudice et al.42. evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of PR and CBCT images in assessing endodontic treatment results. The authors analyzed 101 patients with previous endodontic treatments who underwent both PR and CBCT imaging. CBCT has proven to be a more accurate diagnostic tool for endodontic problems than conventional intraoral radiographs are able to detect important radiological signs not always visible in periapical X-rays, particularly short fillings and untreated canals (up to 30.6%). A recent study by Keerthana et al.43. evaluated PR and CBCT images in the assessment of the endodontic status of 112 teeth. This study revealed that CBCT has greater diagnostic accuracy in diagnosing complex endodontic pathoses than does PR. However, CBCT failed to detect apicomarginal bone defects in 33% of teeth, and limited-FOV CBCT should be considered for select cases where the PR has diagnostic ambiguity. Our results are consistent with this general observation at the level of diagnostic agreement: when benchmarked against CBCT reader consensus, platform performance was higher on CBCT than on PAN for the evaluated post-endodontic radiographic features. However, the present study does not evaluate clinical indications for CBCT, downstream management decisions, cost-effectiveness, or patient outcomes; therefore, these data should not be interpreted as evidence that CBCT is required or universally preferable in clinical care. Our study demonstrated the excellent diagnostic accuracy of the AI platform Diagnocat in the evaluation of CBCT root-treatment outcomes. These findings are consistent with those of previous studies, which reported diagnostic accuracy values exceeding 90%21,24,44,45,46,47. In a 2024 study, the diagnostic performance of Diagnocat was evaluated via 55 CBCT scans23. The authors reported comparable diagnostic accuracy but noted lower accuracy for void detection in fillings (accuracy = 88.6%, precision = 88.9%, recall = 66.7%, F1 = 76.2%), indicating areas for further improvement. Our study also confirmed that diagnostic accuracy notably decreased when Diagnocat was applied to PAN images. This finding is consistent with the 2024 study evaluating AI performance on panoramic radiographs alone, where substantial variability in diagnostic performance was reported. Specifically, lower diagnostic accuracy metrics were noted for assessing adequate obturation and density on PAN images23. Recent ML studies on complex canal morphology, such as the detection of mesio-buccal (MB) canals, further illustrate the value of 3D information for AI-assisted endodontics48. As MB prevalence and detectability affect treatment completeness, such advances are complementary to our findings that CBCT-based AI achieves markedly higher accuracy than PAN for post-treatment features. The limitations inherent in two-dimensional imaging modalities, including superimposition of anatomical structures, lower resolution, and geometric distortions, significantly contribute to these findings. In both the PAN and CBCT analyses, the program exhibited the lowest diagnostic reliability when the “adequate density” parameter was assessed (F1 scores of 42.67% and 84.93%, respectively). This outcome is attributable primarily to the manner in which the program operates: the “adequate density” parameter depends on both the evaluation of the filling’s density and the assessment of any voids within the filling. Consequently, whenever the program’s assessment of the filling density or the presence of voids differed from the reference analysis, a corresponding decrease in diagnostic reliability was observed for the “adequate density” parameter. The same correlation was observed for the parameters short filling, overfilling, and adequate obturation. In instances where these classes were misdiagnosed, the AI program also misjudged the “adequate obturation” parameter. A potential explanation for the discrepancy between our results and those of that study may be the ongoing advancements in Diagnocat’s algorithms, leading to progressively improved performance. Indeed, earlier publications on Diagnocat’s accuracy reported significantly lower metrics than those reported in our study. For example, in a 2021 investigation by Ezhov et al.21., the authors assessed Diagnocat’s diagnostic accuracy across a variety of dental applications via CBCT. Their results showed comparatively lower sensitivity for detecting overfilled (78.31%) and short-filled (69.81%) root canals. Similarly, improvements have been observed in the analysis of PAN images. An initial study by Zadrożny et al.46. demonstrated suboptimal performance for diagnosing root canal fillings, with reported sensitivities for short filling and overfilling of 60.9% and 45.5%, respectively. In contrast, our recent evaluation yielded recall values of over 93% for these same parameters, underscoring the enhanced diagnostic capability of the current iteration of the platform. The increase in diagnostic performance metrics may be attributed to improvements in the algorithm itself. Many authors have noted that the program achieves excellent specificity, exceeding 90% in diagnostic assessments. However, its sensitivity has remained relatively low overall21,22,23,24,45,46,47,49,50. The authors attributed this outcome to the AI platform’s excessive “conservativeness,” whereby minimizing the number of false positives comes at the cost of a higher incidence of false negatives. However, to reliably assess this issue, it would be necessary to conduct a detailed meta-analysis, including meta-regression, that takes into account the year of publication. Our findings indicate that although the readers and the AI tool demonstrated comparable diagnostic performance in PAN assessments relative to the CBCT reference standard, the AI tool’s diagnostic performance measures were substantially lower when compared directly to the readers’ PAN assessments (Table 4). These results clearly suggest that the use of PAN images for radiological evaluation of endodontic treatment features results in considerably greater variability between the human reader and the AI tool than do assessments based on CBCT. A similar conclusion was reported in a recent study that analyzed the presence of periapical lesions in PAN and CBCT images obtained from the same group of patients45. Both sets of images were analyzed by AI software and by three experienced clinicians. The AI tool’s sensitivity in the detection of PLs for PAN images was only 33.33%. For the CBCT images, the AI’s sensitivity was 77.78%. However, the AI specificity was greater than 98% for both the PAN and the CBCT images, again indicating the high “conservativeness” of the AI algorithms in PL detection. The imaging protocols analyzed in this retrospective cohort were not endodontic-optimized. Panoramic radiography is limited by anatomic superimposition and relatively low spatial resolution, whereas the CBCT acquisition used in our center (10 × 13 cm FOV; 0.3 mm voxel) reflects routine indications rather than a dedicated small-FOV, high-resolution endodontic protocol. Prior work demonstrates that visualization of cracks and fine endodontic structures—particularly near high-density materials—is highly dependent on scanner model, acquisition parameters, and FOV and may be substantially impaired by artefacts (Pinto et al.51. Accordingly, subtle endodontic findings may have been under-detected in both modalities, especially in teeth with radiopaque restorations or endodontic materials, and the diagnostic performance reported here should be interpreted in this context and not directly generalized to “ideal” endodontic CBCT conditions. This study has several further limitations that warrant consideration. First - this study was conducted at a single center with a limited set of scanners, acquisition/reconstruction parameters, and referral patterns. While this improves internal consistency, it may limit generalizability because both reader- and AI-performance can vary across vendors/models, reconstruction and post-processing pipelines, voxel size/FOV, dose settings, and local case-mix (prevalence/spectrum, materials, artefact burden), potentially introducing spectrum effects and domain shift. Therefore, our estimates should be interpreted as performance under our institutional conditions and may not directly extrapolate to centers with different populations, indications, or imaging protocols. Another limitation relates to the proprietary nature of the model development data. Beyond the vendor’s high-level statement that the system was trained on > 35,000 dental radiographs, the size, diversity, and representativeness of the training data (patient demographics, disease spectrum, imaging devices, and acquisition protocols) are not available for independent verification. Limited transparency on training data diversity may affect the interpretability and transportability of performance estimates. Third, while CBCT serves as the reference standard, it is not infallible; diagnostic interpretations may still be subject to observer variability despite consensus readings. In addition, we did not correlate imaging findings with clinical signs/symptoms, procedural details, follow-up status, or treatment success/failure; consequently, our results cannot be used to infer outcome benefit, appropriateness of CBCT indications, or a clinical “need” for three-dimensional imaging. Finally, the relatively low prevalence of some assessed features (e.g., voids in fillings) may have impacted the stability of diagnostic metrics, and larger multicenter studies are needed to confirm these results. Future studies could build on our findings by extending validation to multicenter cohorts that include a wider range of scanners, acquisition protocols, and patient case-mix, which would further support generalizability across routine practice settings. In addition, incorporating more readers from multiple dental specialties (e.g., endodontists, general dentists, and dentomaxillofacial radiologists) and a broader range of experience levels could provide a more comprehensive assessment of reproducibility and clinical applicability. Where feasible, future work may also explore alternative consensus/adjudication strategies and report agreement metrics, as well as stratify results by clinically relevant imaging factors (e.g., protocol type and artefact burden), to better characterize performance across different real-world conditions. In routine workflows, AI tools may provide standardized, rapid second-read style output that could assist documentation and consistency of radiographic feature reporting. Nevertheless, the present work evaluates only diagnostic agreement with a reader reference standard and does not measure clinical decision impact, time savings, cost-effectiveness, or patient-level outcomes. The main practical implication of our findings is that platform performance is strongly modality-dependent under the studied protocols: agreement was higher on CBCT than on PAN. Accordingly, any clinical use of AI outputs should remain adjunctive to expert interpretation and should be contextualized to the modality, acquisition parameters, and artefact burden. Clinicians should exercise caution and consider integrating AI primarily as an adjunct to, rather than a replacement for, human expertise—particularly when CBCT imaging is unavailable. However, this approach is still a standard approach in AI-assisted diagnosis52. Future work should explore the real-world impact of AI adoption on clinical decision-making, cost-effectiveness, and patient satisfaction. The evaluated AI platform delivers highly reliable assessment of obturation quality on CBCT and performs on par with experienced clinicians on panoramic images, albeit with reduced sensitivity. However, the platform’s limited diagnostic accuracy in panoramic imaging reflects the inherent constraints of two-dimensional modalities and does not differ from the diagnostic accuracy of human readers. Materials and methods The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki and approved by the Bioethics Committee of the Collegium Medicum, Nicolaus Copernicus University in Torun, Poland (protocol No. KB 274/2025, date 23.04.2025). Owing to the retrospective nature of the study, the need for informed consent was waived by the ethics committee. This observational study was written according to the Preferred Reporting Items for Diagnostic Accuracy Studies in Endodontics (PRIDASE) 2024 and Standards for Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD) guidelines53,54,55. This study was preregistered in the osf.io registry (https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/AJPQ6). Patients The population of this retrospective diagnostic accuracy study initially consisted of 264 (176 females and 88 males) consecutive patients referred for PAN and CBCT imaging at a private dental center. The mean age of all participants was 29.53 years (SD 13.13, range 8–70). All patients had both sets of imaging data acquired in the same office. The patients were referred to both imaging modalities by orthodontists or dental surgeons between January 2023 and March 2025. After the initial diagnostic PAN images were obtained, the selected patients were referred for CBCT scans. The primary indications for large-FOV (10 × 13 cm) CBCT imaging were suspicions of PLs in the PAN images or the presence of impacted teeth on both sides of the dental arches. The main inclusion criterion of the stud was the availability of both PAN and CBCT images taken within a 30-day interval. A short time period was used to minimize the impact of different factors on patients’ dental status. The main exclusion criterion was that the scan did not cover all the present teeth fully. Scans with severe motion artifacts and poor overall image quality were also excluded. After the initial selection of patients with both PAN and CBCT images, 85 patients were excluded because of the extended time interval between the PAN and CBCT scans. Ten scans were excluded because of severe motion artifacts. The authors reviewed both datasets (PAN and CBCT) of 169 patients. Six patients were excluded because the scan region did not cover the entire tooth root. Finally, 163 patients were included in the final study group. Image acquisition All the CBCT and PAN images were acquired via a Hyperion X9 PRO (MyRay, Imola, Italy) machine. One standard, marked as the “Regular” setting of the apparatus, was used to obtain CBCT images (90 kV, 36 mAs, CTDI/Vol 4.09 mGy, and 13 cm FOV). All the CBCT images were reconstructed with a slice thickness of 0.3 mm. Patient identifiers were removed to maintain anonymity, and images were coded for blinded analysis. AI evaluation. In this study, we evaluated a commercial AI platform developed by Diagnocat Ltd. (San Francisco), which is based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) for automated dental image analysis. According to vendor-provided documentation, the system was trained on > 35,000 dental radiographs and includes dedicated tools for detecting multiple findings. Detailed information on the training dataset composition (e.g., geographic distribution, scanner vendors/protocols, demographic characteristics, and case spectrum) is not publicly disclosed and cannot be independently audited within this study. Both datasets (PAN and CBCT) of images were manually uploaded to Diagnocat web-platform. For CBCT, the complete DICOM volume dataset (all slices/series constituting the scan) was uploaded to the platform; no pre-selection of teeth or slices was performed. The AI software automatically generated reports that estimated the probabilities (0–100%) of various conditions. For endodontic treatment assessments, the AI evaluated the following features: 1. Presence of filling 2. Adequate obturation 3. Adequate density 4. Overfilling 5. Voids in filling 6. Short filling The platform Diagnocat on elementary level utilizes a binary classification system to evaluate the occurrence of lesions or conditions. In the comprehensive reports generated, this binary classification is further supplemented by probability outputs that range from 0 to 100%. The artificial intelligence system applies this predefined threshold of 50% to categorize these outputs, whereby probabilities exceeding 50% are classified as positive. The platform processes PAN and CBCT using modality-specific pipelines (i.e., separate internal workflows optimized for each modality). Accordingly, PAN and CBCT were analyzed independently, and all performance estimates are presented in modality-stratified form. Any cross-modality contrasts in this manuscript refer to differences in observed platform output performance by modality. The results of the AI endodontic treatment assessments were manually extracted into two separate spreadsheets (PAN and CBCT). Multireader evaluation The images were independently evaluated by two readers, one general dentist and one radiologist, both with more than 8 years of experience. The reading sessions were performed on a dedicated console via iRYS Viewer 6.2 (MyRay, Italy) software. CBCT volumes were assessed dynamically using full multi planar reconstructions (axial/coronal/sagittal scrolling and reformatting) with adjustable display settings (brightness/contrast). During CBCT analysis, the viewer’s initial window width and level were standardized (width 1048; level 4096) using the software’s vendor-specific gray-value scale (not true calibrated Hounsfield Units). All the images were evaluated via a RadiForce MX243W monitor (Eizo, Japan), which is certified for medical use. The reading sessions were conducted in a CT reporting room without access to sunlight and with dimmed light to ensure appropriate conditions for the evaluation of radiological examinations. The Readers had no access to patients’ clinical data. The presence of root canal fillings and the features listed in the AI reports were recorded for each tooth. The following features were assessed: 1. Presence of filling—the presence of radiopaque filling material within the root canal system. 2. Adequate Obturation—complete filling of the root canal system from the coronal reference point to a point near the radiographic apex, ensuring minimal gaps or voids. 3. Adequate density—uniform radiopacity of the filling material throughout its length. 4. Overfilling—the filling material extends beyond the radiographic apex. 5. Voids in filling—radiolucent spaces within the root canal filling material. 6. Short filling—filling that does not extend to within 2 mm of the radiographic apex. The readers were blinded to each other’s assessments and AI results. The readers initially evaluated the PAN images, followed by the CBCT images. The PAN and CBCT evaluation sessions were conducted at least one month apart to avoid potential bias from the PAN reading session. All endodontically treated teeth present in the included scans were eligible for analysis, irrespective of arch or tooth group (anterior/posterior). The unit of analysis was the individual tooth. After independent reads, any discrepancies were resolved in a consensus session; the consensus on CBCT constituted the reference standard. This consensus on CBCT images was considered the reference standard, as three-dimensional imaging assessed by experienced observers represents the most accurate method currently available for evaluating these radiological features2. To assess the reliability of the AI diagnostic reports, they were compared with the consensus reached by the observers. Statistical evaluation The diagnostic performance of the AI program was assessed against the common reference method (readers’ consensus CBCT analysis) and is reported separately for CBCT and PAN. The means, standard deviations, medians, quartiles and ranges of quantitative variables are shown. For qualitative variables, absolute and relative frequencies (N and %) are reported. The accuracy, precision, sensitivity (recall) and F1 score were calculated. The 95% confidence intervals (95% CIs) of the diagnostic accuracy metrics were calculated. Confidence intervals were estimated using non-parametric bootstrap resampling at the tooth level. The formulas used in diagnostic performance calculations and further explanations can be found in Hicks et al.57. The significance level was set to 0.05. All the analyses were conducted in R software, version 4.5.1.

Q: How is Dentalia transforming dental healthcare in Mexico, and what have been its main contributions to the field?

A: Dentalia was founded 20 years ago by Federico Weber with the objective of transforming access to dental care in Mexico. At its inception, the company focused on a clinical care model built around physical dental clinics. The central question was how to deliver dental services that were both accessible and convenient while maintaining high quality standards. From the beginning, clinics were located in shopping centers, operated nearly year-round, and were designed to be financially accessible to a broad segment of the population. This model responded to significant structural challenges in Mexico. Culturally, the country has a limited preventive health mindset, and dental care utilization is particularly low. Dental visits among the Mexican population are among the least frequent in Latin America, with many individuals visiting a dentist only once every 8 to 10 years. Even among more engaged segments of the population, visits often occur only once every five years, far below the clinical recommendation of at least one annual visit, with two per year being optimal. At the same time, Mexico faces a shortage of dental professionals relative to its population. The density of dentists per 10,000 inhabitants is among the lowest in the region. With roughly 120,000 dentists nationwide, access to timely and preventive care remains a systemic challenge. Dentalia was created with these structural gaps in mind. Over time, the company evolved from a clinic-centered model into an integrated dental services platform that partners with multiple organizations such as insurance companies, brokers, and companies through corporate dental plans, designed to address prevention, continuity of care, and system-wide accessibility in a structurally underserved market. Q: How does Dentalia create value for companies through its corporate dental plan model?

A: A core component of Dentalia’s integrated model is the provision of dental plans for employers, insurers, and assistance providers, built around what we define as “tangible benefits.” Unlike many traditional insurance products that are rarely used, our dental plans are designed to actively drive high utilization, particularly in preventive care. Our objective is to ensure that dental plan beneficiaries attend regular check-ups, receive timely diagnostics, and undergo preventive treatments such as cleanings and basic procedures that preserve long-term oral health. For companies, this translates into a prevention-driven benefit that employees actually use and value. After life and major medical insurance, dental plans consistently rank among the most appreciated complementary benefits. By promoting preventive dental care, organizations contribute to employee and insured individuals’ wellbeing, engagement, and productivity. Dentalia administers nearly 1.5 million dental plans directly from insurers and companies and supports several million additional beneficiaries through partnerships with assistance providers. One of the main challenges in this segment is lack of awareness, as many beneficiaries do not know their policies include dental coverage. To address this, we work closely with companies through health fairs and communication initiatives to encourage high utilization. Among corporate clients, utilization rates reach about 30%, which is high compared to other employee insurance benefits. Corporate renewal rates exceed 98%, reflecting long-term value creation and sustained trust. Q: How does Dentalia’s clinical care network complement this model and differentiate the patient experience?

A: Dentalia operates about 60 clinics nationwide, supported by a network of over 500 affiliated clinics to ensure geographic coverage, including locations where we do not have a direct presence. Within our own clinics, we focus on delivering a differentiated patient experience built on four main principles: trust, technology, convenience, and clinical quality. Transparency is fundamental. One of the main barriers to dental visits is uncertainty around costs, so we provide clear and visible pricing to give patients certainty about what they will pay. Comprehensive diagnosis is another key element of our value proposition. We use advanced technology, including 360° radiography and intraoral scanners, allowing patients to clearly see and understand their oral health condition. This promotes informed decision-making and reinforces trust. Convenience is equally important. Our clinics operate extended hours, including weekends, and remain open nearly year-round to remove logistical barriers and make it easier for patients to prioritize their oral health. Finally, we ensure that our more than 600 clinicians are trained under standardized protocols and strict quality standards to guarantee consistent clinical excellence and high-quality dental treatments across our entire network. The integration of corporate plans with clinical care creates a virtuous cycle. Beneficiaries use their plans, access preventive and corrective care, improve their oral health, and return regularly. Employers, in turn, see a healthier and more engaged workforce. This positions Dentalia not merely as a network of clinics, but as a long-term partner in advancing preventive dental health in Mexico. Q: How can a greater focus on oral health among the Mexican population contribute to improvements in other areas of public health in the country?

A: One of our key priorities is raising awareness that oral health is directly connected to overall health and wellbeing. Extensive clinical evidence links proper oral care with broader health outcomes and well-being. For example, poor occlusion can lead to digestive complications because food is not processed correctly. Some of the most impactful cases we see involve the early detection of serious diseases during routine dental check-ups, including oral cancer. A patient may come in for a standard cleaning or minor discomfort, and a comprehensive evaluation allows us to identify a much more serious condition at an early, treatable stage. This has a profound impact on individual health, potentially saving lives, while also benefiting the healthcare system, as preventive care is far more effective than treating advanced disease. Changing habits begins with knowledge. Visiting the dentist should not be a luxury; it is a fundamental part of maintaining overall health and building a preventive culture that helps avoid more serious conditions in the future. The challenge lies in fostering this awareness in a population where regular dental visits are not yet a habit. Q: How does Dentalia address the growing demand for aesthetic dental treatments within its broader clinical care model?

A: Within our clinical care model, we operate as a comprehensive dental provider. This includes pediatric dentistry, periodontics, orthodontics, and maxillofacial surgery, among others. Our clinics are designed to provide complete dental care for patients of all ages and needs in one place. This also includes aesthetic treatments. While our approach always begins with a thorough clinical diagnosis, we fully support patients who wish to improve their self-confidence and are interested in cosmetic procedures such as teeth whitening or dental alignment. We work with leading international suppliers and high-quality materials, allowing us to offer treatment plans that integrate both clinical and aesthetic needs. Q: How does your integration of AI solutions such as Diagnocat enhance diagnostic accuracy and patient care across Dentalia’s clinics?

A: Diagnocat is an AI-powered technology that Dentalia is currently rolling out to enhance the accuracy and clarity of dental diagnoses. The platform analyzes patients’ radiographic images and compares them against millions of cases, enabling the detection of conditions that may be difficult to identify with the human eye alone. Its ability to distinguish subtle variations in imaging supports more precise clinical evaluations. Diagnocat serves as a complementary diagnostic tool. Dentists conduct their clinical examination and initial assessment, which is then supported by AI analysis. This dual approach increases diagnostic certainty, strengthens patient trust, and helps ensure consistency in clinical quality. It also helps prevent both overdiagnosis and underdiagnosis by providing an additional layer of verification. Beyond clinical accuracy, the technology improves efficiency and patient experience. It assists clinicians in developing treatment plans more quickly and presents findings in a highly visual and easy-to-understand format, making it a valuable educational tool. Patients can clearly see highlighted areas of concern, which promotes understanding, awareness, and acceptance of treatment recommendations. Finally, Diagnocat integrates with Dentalia’s systems, supporting standardized records, follow-up, and continuity of care, while reinforcing a data-driven and preventive approach to oral health. Q: What are Dentalia’s priorities and main goals for 2026, and what would make the year a successful one?

A: Dentalia has defined a 2028 strategic roadmap called the “1–2–3 Vision,” which will guide its 2026 efforts. The first pillar centers on consolidation as a fully integrated dental services organization, serving both patients and corporate clients through an exceptional, forward-looking care experience. This means operating as “One Dentalia” culturally and operationally. The second pillar is growth. The company aims to foster revenue growth by expanding its corporate client base, increasing the number of beneficiaries served, and driving higher patient recurrence. Having treated about 180,000 patients in 2025, Dentalia seeks to significantly increase that figure while ensuring that at least 60% of annual visits come from returning patients. While patient satisfaction remains strong, with a high sector NPS, recurrence is the most meaningful indicator of trust, continuity of care, and preventive behavior. The third pillar focuses on multiplying impact. Dentalia aims to achieve sustainable improvements in profitability through operational efficiency and the use of technology across the value chain, from appointment scheduling and reporting to training and diagnostics. At the same time, the company seeks to accelerate patients’ progress in their treatment plans and overall oral health outcomes by delivering dental treatments with Mexico’s top clinical talent. Ultimately, the ambition goes beyond corporate growth. The 1–2–3 Vision reflects the belief that scale, integration, and impact must advance together. By operating as one integrated dental platform and expanding access through prevention and technology, Dentalia aims to help shift oral health in Mexico from episodic treatment toward normalized prevention as a public-health standard, improving quality of life and reducing long-term health burdens at scale.
