data.title: Detection accuracy of an AI platform for dental treatment features on panoramic radiographs – tooth- and patient-level analyses
data.ai_summary: A retrospective study evaluated the commercial AI platform Diagnocat (Diagnocat Inc., San Francisco) for detecting dental treatment features on panoramic radiographs using 147 patients with 4,148 teeth, finding high tooth-level accuracy (94.9–99.9%) for most features but a significantly lower patient-level "perfect match" accuracy of only 56.5% when requiring error-free full-mouth reports. The most common errors stemmed from fillings (57.3% of discrepancies) and endodontic treatments (19.5%), with posterior teeth showing higher error rates due to anatomical superimposition and structural overlap. The study concludes that while the AI platform is suitable as an assistive "second reader" tool, it is not yet reliable enough for autonomous diagnostic charting, and clinician oversight remains essential.
data.author: Kazimierczak
data.full_text:
Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) has shown promise in dental imaging, yet its reliability for comprehensive diagnostic charting from panoramic radiographs (PAN) remains uncertain. We evaluated the diagnostic performance of a commercial AI platform (Diagnocat™, San Francisco, USA) in detecting common dental treatment features on PAN images. In this retrospective study, 147 patients (4,148 teeth) were analyzed against the consensus of two experienced readers. Tooth-level performance was assessed for missing teeth, fillings, crowns, pontics, endodontic treatments, orthodontic appliances, and implants, using patient-clustered nonparametric bootstrapping used to account for within-patient correlations. At the tooth level, the AI achieved high diagnostic accuracy across features (94.9–99.9%), with nearly perfect results for missing teeth, crowns, pontics, and implants. However, under a stringent patient-level “perfect match” criterion requiring error-free full-mouth reports, the AI succeeded in only 56.5% of cases (95% CI, 48.4–64.2%). Errors were most often related to fillings (57.3%) and endodontic treatments (19.5%). These findings highlight a critical gap between high per-tooth accuracy and clinically meaningful patient-level performance. These findings underscore that while the AI performs strongly at the tooth level, its patient-level performance is insufficient for autonomous diagnostic charting.

Introduction The digital transformation of dental imaging—marked by the routine use of panoramic radiography (PAN) and the rapid adoption of cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT)—has enabled precise diagnostics and tailored treatment plans. However, this level of precision also requires clinicians to possess high diagnostic skills. Computer-aided diagnosis (CAD) is a rapidly developing field in medical imaging that facilitates the detection of diverse conditions. It has gained significant momentum in the past few years, following the broad introduction of artificial intelligence (AI). Deep learning (DL), a subdivision of AI, has been used for more than 10 years to match or surpass human performance in fundamental image analysis tasks such as classification, object detection, and segmentation1. The application of such systems in dental imaging has allowed the creation of commercially available chairside software, generating automated dental charts and structured reports2. PAN enables detailed visualization of the entire dentomaxillofacial region at a low radiation dose with a single exposition. However, their inherent two-dimensional (2D) projection, superimposition and geometric distortion can obscure subtle lesions and treatment-related findings3,4,5. In addition, research has indicated that examiners with greater experience achieve greater diagnostic accuracy than do their less experienced counterparts6. Despite this issue, owing to its wide availability and low cost, PAN remains the most frequently prescribed extraoral examination in dentistry7. Accurate identification of previous dental interventions, such as root canal fillings, posts and cores, crowns, implants, orthodontic braces and other restorative materials, is essential for documentation, treatment planning, follow-up and forensic identification. Bringing AI support to this task promises greater diagnostic consistency and workflow efficiency across imaging techniques8. Previous research has demonstrated the potential of DL algorithms to automatically detect and classify various dental restorations on PAN images with high accuracy9,10. While challenges remain, particularly with restorations having radiodensities similar to tooth structure or appearing as fine details, the potential for AI to enhance diagnostic consistency and efficiency is evident10. Diagnocat™ (Diagnocat Inc., San Francisco, USA) is a commercially available, widely used, cloud-based AI solution that provides automated detection and annotation of dental findings on CBCT images, periapical radiographs, and PAN images. Diagnocat™ is one of the most widely adopted AI platforms in Europe for panoramic, periapical, and CBCT imaging, and is currently used in several clinical centers and tele-radiology workflows. In Poland, Diagnocat is among the most frequently implemented CE-marked commercial systems, which makes its real-world reliability highly clinically relevant compared to other available systems (e.g., Algin X-ray Insights, WeDiagnostiX). In addition to simple feature detection, the automation of the diagnostic process significantly reduces the time required for radiographic interpretation, thereby enhancing clinical workflow efficiency11. Despite the promising findings related to the use of this AI platform in CBCT analysis12,13,14,15,16, the reliability of the program in evaluating PAN images remains markedly lower17,18,19,20. Moreover, the platform’s reliability has not been comprehensively established against an expert consensus on a large cohort of patients exceeding 100 subjects17,18,19,20. While previous work has assessed specific features, a comprehensive and rigorous evaluation of the platform’s ability to identify a wide array of common dental treatments simultaneously, which is crucial for automated charting, has not been fully established against an expert consensus. Furthermore, while previous work has assessed specific features at the tooth level, a critical gap exists in evaluating the platform’s ability to generate a completely accurate, full-mouth diagnostic report—a prerequisite for trustworthy automated charting. High tooth-level accuracy does not necessarily translate to perfect patient-level performance, as even a small error rate can lead to a high probability of at least one error on a full-mouth scan. Therefore, the aim of this study is twofold: first, to evaluate the tooth-level accuracy of the Diagnocat AI platform in detecting common dental treatment signs on PAN images, and second, to introduce a stringent patient-level analysis to assess its reliability for producing a completely error-free, full-mouth diagnosis. Results Patient characteristics A total of 147 patients with 4148 teeth were included in the final analysis. The mean age of the participants was 34.46 years (SD = 13.29), ranging from 11 to 70 years. The median age was 33 years (quartile range 24.5–43.5). Most of the patients were female (65.99%; n = 97), whereas 34.01% (n = 50) were male. STARD flow diagram of the study material is shown in Fig. 1. The study group characteristics can be found in Table 1. A summary of the findings is presented in Table 2. Table 1 Characteristics of the study group. Full size table Table 2 Summary of dental treatment findings. Full size table Fig. 1 STARD flow diagram of the study material. Full size image No indeterminate results were encountered. All AI and reference assessments were categorical and conclusive. There were no missing data for index or reference test outcomes after initial exclusions. Owing to the retrospective nature of the study, no adverse events were associated with performing the index or reference tests. Interreader agreement The initial agreement was found to be substantial to nearly perfect across most categories, including missing teeth (κ = 0.98), crowns (κ = 0.95), pontics (κ = 0.99), orthodontic appliances, implants (κ = 1.00), fillings (κ = 0.91), and endodontic treatments (κ = 0.89). Most discrepancies among the readers stemmed from minor errors in tooth numbering rather than from any disagreement regarding the presence of dental treatment features. Tooth-level detection accuracy The detection accuracy of the Diagnocat AI platform was evaluated on the basis of the following dental treatment signs: filling, missing teeth, orthodontic appliance, endodontics, crown, implants and pontic. Because all 14 implants were correctly diagnosed, each of the software’s diagnostic accuracy metrics (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, and overall accuracy) was 100%. However, owing to the limited sample size (n = 14), those results are not shown in the figures and tables. The diagnostic performance of the remaining assessed features is summarized in Table 3. Table 3 Detection accuracy metrics with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Full size table A visual representation of the detection accuracy measures with corresponding 95% confidence intervals is provided in Fig. 2, clearly illustrating the high performance of the AI platform across the evaluated dental treatments. Fig. 2 Detection accuracy metrics with 95% confidence intervals (bars). Full size image Figures. 3 and 4 present sample misdiagnoses of endodontic treatment. Fig. 3 False positive diagnosis of endodontically treated tooth 15 caused by superimposition of bony structures (red arrow). Full size image Fig. 4 Sample false positive endodontic treatment diagnoses (orange arrows): A - tooth 27, 30-year-old male; B - tooth 46, 28-year-old male; C - tooth 35, 57-year-old female. D - sample of false negative endodontic treatment diagnosis (red arrow) - tooth 12, 52-year-old female. Full size image Anatomical distribution of AI errors Error distribution demonstrated a clear spatial pattern across the dentition. Posterior teeth—particularly maxillary molars (teeth 15, 16, 24, 26, 27) and mandibular molars (35, 36, 37, 47, 48)—showed the highest discrepancy counts (7–11 errors per tooth position), whereas anterior teeth exhibited near-zero error frequency (0–3 discrepancies). This pattern was visualized using a per-tooth heatmap (Fig. 5), which confirmed distinct “hot zones” of diagnostic difficulty in posterior regions. These findings are consistent with known PAN imaging limitations, including: superimposition of the zygomatic bones over maxillary molars,

overlapping multi-rooted structures,

cervical spine ghost shadows near mandibular molars,

reduced contrast and anatomical noise in the posterior zones. In contrast, the anterior region benefited from clearer visualization and showed markedly fewer discrepancies. Fig. 5 Per-tooth discrepancies heatmap. Full size image Distribution of discrepancies A total of 307 individual tooth-level discrepancies were identified across the 122 incorrect patient cases. The distributions of these errors are presented in Table 4. The analysis revealed that errors related to fillings were by far the most significant contributors to patient-level failure, accounting for 57.3% of all discrepancies. The second most common cause was endodontic treatment, which was responsible for 19.5% of the discrepancies. Table 4 Frequency and type of discrepancy contributing to patient-level failures. Full size table Parsing multi-label annotations revealed systematic misclassification tendencies: Endodontics \(\leftrightarrow\) Posts/cores : The most common qualitative error source, with radiopaque posts interpreted as root canal fillings and vice versa.

Fillings \(\leftrightarrow\) Crowns : Metal-ceramic crowns with large cores were sometimes identified as extensive restorations rather than crowns.

Crown \(\leftrightarrow\) Pontic : Splinted or fused crowns occasionally triggered false-positive pontic detections.

Posterior composite fillings: Low radiopacity contributed to false negatives. To quantify the impact of tooth location on diagnostic performance, an exploratory logistic regression model was fitted with error presence (yes/no) as the outcome and molar status as the main predictor. Molars were associated with significantly higher odds of AI error (OR = 2.12; 95% CI: 1.51–2.97; p < 0.001), supporting the anatomical findings above. This association likely reflects the combined effect of structural overlap, increased anatomical complexity, and projection-related artifacts. Patient-level accuracy results The AI system produced an exact per-patient treatment map in 56.5% (83/147) of the cases (95% CI, 48.4–64.2%). Allowing for minor discrepancies, 80.9% of patients had ≤ 1 error, and 87.8% had ≤ 2 errors per patient. The patient-level detection results are summarized in Table 5. Table 5 Detection accuracy in the detection of dental treatment signs at the patient level – “perfect-match”. Full size table The results of the basic “per-feature” detection accuracy analysis are summarized in Table 6. In a “per-feature”, patient-level analysis (features considered positive if present on ≥ 1 tooth), detection was highest for treatment-critical findings: missing teeth (sensitivity 100.0%, PPV 97.37%), implants (100/100%), and endodontic treatment (100/98.84%). The performance for fillings (100/99.29%) and crowns (91.3/100%) remained high, as did pontics and orthodontic appliances (both 100/100%). Table 6 Per-feature, patient-level performance. Full size table Discussion This study provides a dual-faceted evaluation of a commercial AI platform, revealing a significant disparity between its performance at the tooth level and the patient level. At the tooth level, the AI achieved a high overall accuracy of over 94.9% across all six categories, with nearly flawless performance in detecting missing teeth, crowns, and pontics. These findings are consistent with a rapidly expanding body of literature demonstrating that AI systems can rival or exceed human performance in discrete radiological tasks21,22,23,24,25,26,27. However, the central finding of this study is the AI’s substantially lower accuracy of 56.5% when evaluated under a stringent patient-level criterion, where a diagnosis is considered correct only if it is entirely free of errors across the full dentition. This discrepancy highlights a critical gap in the current validation of diagnostic AI tools in dentistry. While high-tooth-level metrics suggest reliability, they do not capture the cumulative probability of error across an entire patient case. A single missed finding or false positive can alter a treatment plan, making 100% accuracy the ultimate goal for autonomous charting. Our patient-level analysis demonstrated that even with high per-tooth accuracy, the likelihood of achieving a perfect full-mouth report is low. This suggests that most studies, which focus solely on tooth-level metrics, may present an overly optimistic view of the clinical readiness of these tools for fully autonomous use. The single-tooth assessments most commonly used to date should be supplanted by more holistic, patient-level evaluations to provide a more realistic measure of clinical utility. Our findings at the granular tooth level align with the rapidly expanding body of literature on the application of AI in various areas of dentistry, including periodontology, orthodontics, conservative dentistry, and dental radiology21,22,23,24,25,26,27. Owing to its high level of digitization and the nature of radiological assessments, dental radiology is the field most predisposed to the implementation of AI systems. This observation is consistent with the broader trend in traditional radiology, where medical imaging accounts for approximately 85% of FDA-approved AI programs (data from 2023)28. In the field of dentomaxillofacial radiology, several AI-based systems have been developed to analyze two-dimensional images—examples include Denti. Ai, Overjet, and Pearl. Several platforms, such as Diagnocat and Relu, are also capable of evaluating three-dimensional CBCT images. However, given the growing number of users, it is imperative to rigorously and scientifically verify the diagnostic reliability of these systems to safeguard the well-being of patients whose examinations are analyzed by these platforms worldwide. Although multiple commercial platforms exist, published diagnostic accuracy data remain limited, and none include dual-level accuracy assessment; therefore, our results offer unique comparative value. Two-dimensional (2D) radiographic imaging presents inherent limitations, including superimposition of anatomical structures, geometric distortion, anatomical noise, and restricted dimensionality29. Additional challenges, such as low contrast and poorly defined tooth margins, further impede diagnostic accuracy30. These limitations contribute to interobserver variability and necessitate cautious interpretation. These constraints equally affect PAN imaging and periapical radiography (PR), which often lack the resolution necessary for detailed assessments. Consequently, clinicians frequently prefer PRs or CBCT for detailed evaluations31,32. Nonetheless, PAN remains a widely used initial screening tool in dental practice because of its versatility, low cost and high availability. Error patterns indicated that anatomical noise in posterior regions, radiopaque restorative materials, and structural overlap were major contributors to inaccuracies of AI platform. These findings align with known limitations of panoramic imaging and highlight areas where targeted algorithmic retraining may significantly improve performance. Given the systematic nature of certain errors, retraining or fine-tuning algorithms using misclassified cases—particularly posterior teeth and complex restorative situations—could meaningfully improve accuracy. Future collaboration with industry partners may facilitate such refinements. Numerous studies have demonstrated that AI systems—especially those based on DL—achieve high accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity in identifying dental fillings, often rivaling or surpassing the performance of human clinicians19,33,34,35,36,37,38. For example, recent research reported F1 scores and accuracy rates above 90% for the detection of fillings and other restorations, with some models achieving near-perfect agreement with expert annotations34,37,38. However, some authors have shown that the diagnostic performance can vary depending on the type of filling (e.g., metal-based vs. resin-based) and the patient population (e.g., adults vs. pediatric patients)33,38,39. Although our study group included patients across a wide age range (11–70 years) and included both composite and amalgam restorations, the AI platform demonstrated excellent performance in detecting fillings, with a sensitivity of 91.2%. Although PANs provide a broad overview of the maxillofacial region, their ability to detect fine details is limited40. Nonetheless, they are reliable for evaluating parameters such as the number of remaining and root-filled teeth (19). In the present study, our results demonstrated almost perfect alignment between the readers’ consensus and the AI platform in detecting missing teeth (sensitivity = 99.1%). However, the AI platform showed lower detection accuracy in identifying endodontically treated teeth (sensitivity = 88.6%). This reduction in accuracy may be attributed to the inherent subtlety of radiographic indicators of root canal filling, which can be obscured by overlapping structures or variations in material density. Conversely, superimposition of bony structures can also mimic signs of root canal therapy (Fig. 3). These challenges affect both human observers and AI algorithms, making endodontic assessment particularly demanding. The slightly lower, although still clinically excellent, sensitivity for detecting endodontic treatments (88.6%) is also a recurring theme in similar studies on PAN images17,41. Kazimierczak et al.. reported a sensitivity of 90.7% for endodontically treated teeth17. However, the authors evaluated only 55 PAN images. In a 2022 study, Zadrożny et al.41. explored multiple correlations between the assessments of experienced readers and the Diagnocat AI platform with respect to various features in PAN images. They identified a high level of correlation for endodontic treatment (ICC = 0.948), missing teeth (ICC = 0.959), fillings (ICC = 0.92), and prosthetic materials such as crowns and posts (ICC = 0.968). The authors of both manuscripts concluded that the tested AI system can be beneficial for preliminary evaluation of PAN images, providing reliable results and recommending further diagnostic methods when more precise assessment is needed. In a recent study, Turosz et al.. investigated the diagnostic accuracy of AI software (CS imaging software, Carestream Dental LLC, Atlanta, GA, USA) in the analysis of PAN images42. The authors assessed the program’s accuracy in detecting the location of missing teeth, root canal fillings, endodontic lesions, dental crowns, pontics, implants, and implant abutment crowns. Their findings revealed high performance—exceeding 90% accuracy—in identifying missing teeth, root canal fillings, and implant abutment crowns. In contrast, the software demonstrated moderate sensitivity (94.57%) for detecting endodontic lesions and the lowest sensitivity (80.92%) for identifying pontics. Consistent with previous work by Zadrożny, the authors concluded that AI software can be a valuable tool in clinical practice for diagnosis and treatment planning, although additional verification by clinicians is advisable, particularly for tasks such as the identification of dental crowns. A comparable study conducted in 2022 evaluated the diagnostic reliability of the web-based AI platform Denti.AI using 300 PAN images33. The authors reported substantially lower accuracy in detecting crowns and fillings (89.53% and 56.95%, respectively) than did the previously cited methods and our own findings. The software exhibited particularly low sensitivity in identifying resin-based restorations (41.11%). Nevertheless, its performance in detecting implants and root canal treatments was similar to our results, with reported sensitivities of 100% and 91.9%, respectively. Despite the lower accuracy in detecting fillings, the authors concluded that the examined AI platform can improve overall diagnostic and treatment decisions by minimizing subjectivity and minimizing potential human error. A significant strength of the evaluated AI is its potential to reduce the diagnostic workload and minimize human error, especially for less experienced clinicians37,42,43. The incorporation of AI systems such as the tested platform into routine clinical workflows can streamline radiographic interpretation, particularly in high-volume practices. By automating the detection of previously performed treatments, AI tools reduce the time clinicians spend on repetitive charting tasks, enabling a more focused assessment of pathologies. Furthermore, cloud-based deployment, as exemplified by Diagnocat, facilitates integration with telehealth platforms and remote diagnostics. It enables clinicians to remotely access patients’ images and thus facilitate treatment planning. These advantages underscore the potential of AI to support more efficient, accessible, and patient-centered care in dentistry. However, successful implementation requires institutional commitment, appropriate clinician training, and clear guidelines for interpreting AI outputs within existing diagnostic protocols. Nevertheless, clinician oversight remains essential, particularly for ambiguous or complex cases, and further research is needed to improve AI performance for challenging cases and patient populations33,42,44. As AI becomes increasingly integrated into dental diagnostics, ethical and legal concerns must be addressed. These include ensuring data privacy, managing diagnostic accountability, and avoiding overreliance on automated outputs. Transparent reporting of algorithm limitations and continuous performance monitoring are essential to maintain patient safety and clinical trust. In cases where AI misses a clinically relevant finding, liability remains with the clinician, underscoring the need for transparent communication about AI involvement. Clear documentation in patient records—indicating whether AI assisted in diagnostic interpretation—may become necessary in future regulatory frameworks. Furthemore the frameworks must clearly define clinician responsibility when AI tools are used in diagnostic decision-making45,46. The results of our study position the AI platform as a powerful assistive tool or “second reader” rather than a replacement for a clinician. From a clinical workflow perspective, the platform is best positioned as a pre-screening or parallel ‘second reader’ tool. Clinicians should pay particular attention to features with higher error rates—especially fillings and endodontic treatments—where human verification remains essential. A practical implementation strategy may include AI-generated charting followed by clinician validation of flagged regions or discrepancies, which can improve efficiency without compromising diagnostic safety. The platform can effectively automate routine diagnostic tasks, enhance the efficiency of radiological interpretation, and reduce the risk of oversight for individual findings. However, its inability to consistently generate error-free, full-mouth reports means that clinician oversight remains essential. This nuanced role is critical for managing expectations and ensuring safe and effective integration into clinical workflows. As emphasized by Uribe et al.., continuous performance monitoring and real-world validation are essential for the sustainable implementation of any AI tool47. Despite these promising results, it is important to acknowledge the limitations of this study. One of the primary limitations of this study is the limited number of some of the dental conditions examined, such as implants and pontics, which limits our detection accuracy analyses. The perfect detection of implants and pontics must be interpreted cautiously because of the very small number of positive cases (n = 14 and n = 28, respectively). These estimates inherently carry wide confidence intervals, limiting the ability to draw definitive conclusions about real-world performance. The study was conducted at a single center using a single panoramic unit (Hyperion X9 Pro). The homogeneity of imaging parameters and the specific referral structure (primarily orthodontic and surgical patients) may introduce spectrum bias. Consequently, the AI’s performance may differ in general dentistry populations, mixed-device environments, or images of lower quality. Future studies should aim for a multicenter, prospective design with a consensus panel of multiple experts forming the gold standard to further validate these findings. Additionally, this study focused on treatment features; the AI’s efficacy in detecting carious lesions, periapical pathology, or periodontal disease was not assessed and warrants separate investigation. Another limitation is that intra-observer reliability was not assessed. Although both readers demonstrated substantial to near-perfect inter-observer agreement, repeat readings were not performed. The absence of intra-observer data may reduce the precision of the expert consensus used as the reference standard. This study demonstrated that the evaluated AI software achieves high reliability and accuracy for identifying individual dental treatments on PAN images at the tooth level, with performance comparable to that of experienced readers for discrete tasks. However, the novel and stringent patient-level analysis reveals a “perfect match” accuracy of only 56.5% for producing a completely error-free, full-mouth diagnosis. This critical finding underscores the distinction between a feature-detection tool and a fully autonomous diagnostic system. While the platform holds significant promise for optimizing clinical workflows and improving diagnostic consistency as an assistive tool or “second reader,” it is not yet reliable enough to replace the holistic, integrative assessment of a clinician for final diagnostic charting. Therefore, we conclude that the AI platform is a valuable supplement in dental diagnostics, but meticulous clinical oversight remains indispensable to ensure patient safety and guarantee comprehensive diagnostic accuracy. Materials and methods Study design and ethics approval This is a retrospective, single-center detection accuracy study that evaluates the performance of a commercial AI platform in identifying dental treatment features on PAN images. The study was written according to the Standards for Reporting of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies (STARD) 201548. The study protocol is available upon reasonable request from the corresponding author. Patients This retrospective detection accuracy study initially included 161 consecutive patients referred for PAN imaging at a single private dental center. Patients were referred for PAN imaging by orthodontists or dental surgeons between 01.2024 and 31.03.2025. The PAN serves as the initial imaging modality in surgical and orthodontic patients. The main exclusion criteria were overall poor image quality and the presence of mixed dentition (primary and permanent teeth). After the initial selection of patients, 2 patients were excluded because of poor image quality, and 12 patients were excluded because of the presence of primary teeth. The final analysis included 147 patients. Sample size and precision of estimates This study was designed as an estimation study. Our primary objective was to report point estimates and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) for diagnostic accuracy measures at both the tooth and patient levels. Tooth-level CIs were constructed via patient-clustered nonparametric bootstrapping (3,000 replicates). Patient-level proportions were summarized with nonparametric bootstrap CIs over patients (3,000 replicates). Interreader agreement was summarized with Cohen’s κ and its 95% CI. The achieved CI half-widths for common features (fillings, crowns, endodontic treatments, missing teeth) were within ± 5–10% points, indicating adequate precision for descriptive purposes. Owing to the small number of positive cases, rare features (e.g., pontics and implants) necessarily yield wider CIs. For future studies, ~ 400–450 patients would be required to achieve ≤ 10% point precision for rare features on the basis of observed prevalence and clustering. Image acquisition All the PAN images were acquired via a Hyperion X9 PRO (60–75 kVp, 5–10 mA; MyRay, Imola, Italy) machine. Patient identifiers were removed from all images, and images were coded to ensure blinded analysis. AI evaluation PAN images were uploaded to Diagnocat, a cloud-based AI platform (version 1.0. Diagnocat Ltd., San Francisco, CA, USA). The AI software automatically generated reports indicating the presence and location of various dental treatment signs, including the following: Orthodontic braces.

Prostheses (fixed and removable).

Dental implants.

Signs of endodontic treatment (e.g., root canal fillings, posts).

Restorations (e.g., crowns, fillings). For each identified dental treatment sign, the AI software marked the location and provided a confidence score (0–100%). The program’s threshold for positive diagnosis is a probability of more than 50% lesion/condition occurrence. The AI results for dental treatment sign detection were extracted into the spreadsheet. All the images were uploaded and the analyses were performed within a consistent 10-days interval (April 08–18, 2025) to ensure that no version changes occurred during the evaluation period. Multireader evaluation The PAN images were independently evaluated by two readers, Reader 1, a board-certified radiology specialist, and Reader 2, an orthodontist, both of which have over 10 years of experience in craniofacial image assessment. Reader calibration was performed on 5 images (patients with multiple restorations and mixed endodontic status). Agreement was not assessed. Calibration images were independent from the final study dataset. The reading sessions were conducted on dedicated workstations using syngo.via client ver. 8.9 (Siemens Healthineers, Forchheim, Germany) software. Images were evaluated using a Barco Coronis Fusion 4MP MDCC-4430 (Barco, Kortrijk, Belgium), certified for medical use. The reading environment was standardized with controlled lighting to minimize distractions. Readers assessed the presence or absence of the following dental treatment signs: Orthodontic braces.

Prostheses (fixed and removable).

Dental implants.

Signs of endodontic treatment.

Restorations.

Missing teeth. Each PAN image was independently evaluated by two readers (Reader 1 and Reader 2) who were blinded to the AI results and each other’s findings. The results were recorded in separate spreadsheets. After the initial independent readings, the interreader reliability was calculated for each feature via Cohen’s kappa coefficient. Following this, the readers compared their findings. A third reading session was convened to review the specific case jointly and reach a final consensus on disagreements. This final consensus served as the reference standard for all subsequent analyses. Patient-level success criterion To assess the clinical significance of the results, patient-level analysis was conducted at two levels. 1. “Per feature” - the basic level, patient-level accuracy was defined by whether each treatment feature present in an individual was identified at least once anywhere in the dentition. At this level, minor errors—such as misnumbering or isolated diagnostic mistakes—did not alter the final diagnosis. 2. The “perfect match” approach was designed to assess the AI’s ability to produce a completely accurate, full-mouth diagnostic report—an ultimate requirement for autonomous clinical application. Patient diagnosis was classified as “correct” only if the set of all diagnostic codes for all 32 tooth positions in the AI dataset was perfectly identical to the corresponding set of codes in the reference standard dataset, following the rigorous harmonization protocol: ≤1 error and ≤ 2 errors per patient: number of symmetric-difference tokens ≤ 1 or ≤ 2 across the full mouth. Statistical evaluation The diagnostic performance of the Diagnocat AI platform was evaluated by comparing its findings to the consensus of the two human readers, which served as the reference standard. Performance metrics (sensitivity, specificity, PPV, NPV, accuracy) were computed for six tooth-level categories (missing teeth, fillings, crowns, pontics, endodontic treatment, orthodontic appliances). Because teeth within a patient are not independent, 95% confidence intervals were obtained via a patient-clustered nonparametric bootstrap: patients were resampled with replacement (n = 3,000 replicates), and all teeth belonging to the sampled patients were included within each replicate; percentile intervals were reported. Cells can contain multiple labels (e.g., ‘O, F’), which are parsed so that features can cooccur on a tooth. In a patient-level analysis, presence/absence per feature was defined as positive if the feature occurred on any tooth of the patient; 95% CIs used a nonparametric bootstrap over patients (n = 3,000 replicates). Additionally, an exact match analysis revealed a patient as correct only when the AI exactly matched the reference across all teeth for all six features; CIs for the proportion were obtained via 5,000 patient bootstraps. The interreader reliability was calculated for each feature via Cohen’s kappa coefficient. All the analyses were conducted in R software, version 4.5.1.

data.title: Top Dental Industry Trends in 2025
data.ai_summary: The article discusses key trends in the dental industry for 2025, including advances in digital transformation, AI, 3D printing, staffing solutions, and patient-centric care. It highlights the role of companies like Pearl, Diagnocat, 3Shape, SprintRay, and Teero in shaping these developments.

Uncategorized Staffing Key Dental Industry Trends: What Practice Owners Need to Know In 2025, dental industry trends such as AI and 3D printing technologies, and the increasing consolidation of practices, are keeping practice owners and managers on their toes. Understanding these trends will help you stay competitive and efficient. And with the dental market projected to grow substantially over the coming years, now is the perfect time to use these trends to modernize your practice and embrace the future of dental care. Jan 15, 2025

1. Digital Transformation and Technology Integration





AI and Machine Learning Revolution Dental practices are seeing a big shift as AI and machine learning become essential tools. Leading companies like Pearl, Diagnocat, and 3Shape Automate are transforming diagnostic capabilities through AI-powered analysis of radiographs and intraoral images. AI-powered diagnostic systems can rapidly detect various conditions with high accuracy, from tooth decay to bone loss. AI goes beyond diagnostics; it helps in treatment planning and automation. For example, AI-driven crown design systems can automatically create precise restoration plans, cutting down the planning time significantly while keeping accuracy high. AI also helps in making better decisions by analyzing vast amounts of clinical data to suggest the best treatment approaches. Advanced 3D Printing Applications 3D printing has gone from a novelty to a must-have in dental practices. New advancements now allow for printing permanent restorations. Companies like SprintRay are pioneering innovations in 3D-printed permanent crowns, offering practices the ability to deliver same-day restorations. The technology enables in-house manufacturing of various dental devices, from surgical guides to clear aligners, reducing laboratory costs and treatment times. New dental resins keep expanding what's possible, improving the strength and look of printed restorations. These advancements help practices offer more affordable solutions without sacrificing quality. Home Blog The Top 15 Dental Industry Trends of 2025: What You Need to Know This Year in Dentistry Industry Tech and Innovations July 07, 2025 The Top 15 Dental Industry Trends of 2025: What You Need to Know This Year in Dentistry Wondering what’s next in dentistry? From the newest tech to the most exciting materials, here are the 15 trends that’ll shape how we work in 2025. Dr Sugz Maha General Dentist The dental industry is moving faster than ever. With the latest projections suggesting the US dental market alone could exceed $259.93 billion by 2033 – now is the time to capitalize. Alongside the advancements in technology, growing patient expectations and workforce demands are quietly redefining how dental clinics operate. Whether you’re an orthodontist, a dentist (an owner or an associate), or managing a growing practice, staying ahead of these shifts is crucial. It is becoming increasingly clear that many of these trends I will discuss are here to stay. To be clear, these aren’t vague predictions — they are changes that are actively taking place in clinics, labs, and conversations across the profession. After reading this article, you’ll know: What today’s patients will refuse to compromise on

Which technologies are worth paying attention to (and which you could ignore)

How you can adapt to the biggest potential shift in the profession in the last century

Why strategy matters just as much as clinical skill But, before we dive into the trends, we need to understand the needs of the most important stakeholders in dentistry: our patients. Understanding the Needs of Modern Dental Patients Dental trends can be driven by a variety of factors: venture capital investments, academic institutions, the economy. However, the primary drivers of trends are our patients. Over the last decade, their expectations have shifted. Social media has increased awareness of what’s possible within a clinic. Their tolerance for errors are lower. And, the overall priorities of patients evolved far beyond just a regular six-monthly examination and cleaning. Here’s what they’re really looking for in 2025: Accessibility With hybrid working models, patients need care that fits into their busy schedules. That means flexible hours, easier online booking, and access to late appointments where necessary.



Cost Affordability remains one of the biggest barriers worldwide. Unfortunately, costs of running a clinic are facing an upward trend. As a result, patients are looking for transparency in pricing. Many of them are understanding of these costs, and are willing to seek payment options that won’t catch them off guard.



Quality Concerns With more access to information, patients have become more selective. They expect evidence-based treatment. They will often attend after conducting their own research through social media and AI engines. This means the impetus is placed on clinics to maintain a high standard of care.



Pain and Anxiety Dental anxiety isn’t new, but gone are the days of accepting it as the norm. Today’s patients expect you to actively address it. From sedation options to your communication style, every step matters when it comes to building trust.



Long Waiting Times Following on from the earlier point about accessibility, patients are less willing to wait around. You cannot simply pacify them with a few magazines or a short film in the waiting room. They want efficiency—without feeling rushed—and a clearer sense of how long things will actually take.



Clear Communication Patients will vote with their feet. If they don’t like a dentist, they will make that abundantly clear. Patients expect clarity at every stage, from diagnosis to billing. They want to feel informed, not confused.





At first glance, this list can seem daunting. But, you can meet these needs with ease – especially once you understand how these trends can work to your advantage too. There are three groups of trends that you should be aware of: tech, practice, and patient trends. All of these could have massive impact on you as a clinician in the years moving forward. Dental Tech Trends Dental technology used to be reserved for a select few. It would be something you hear about at a dental conference, or you might have seen a fringe use case a few years ago. In 2025, it is essential for staying competitive in a fast-moving climate. New technologies are transforming how we diagnose, plan, and deliver care. The most crucial point is; patients know about these technologies too. They will see them in action on social media, and begin to expect it when joining a new clinic. In many cases, their expectations have already been shaped by what they’ve already experienced elsewhere—whether it’s a faster turnaround on indirect work, a clearer explanation, or a more comfortable procedure. Here are five technology-driven trends that are changing the game in 2025: 1. 3D Printing Technology 3D printing was once a novelty in dentistry. In its early days, it was written off as a premature, inaccurate innovation. Many dentists felt it was still “a few years away from adoption”. Except, those few years have now flown by. It’s now one of the most impactful technologies in dental labs and clinics, drastically reducing turnaround times for crowns, bridges, dentures, surgical guides, and more. A 2023 report from SmarTech Analysis estimated that the global dental 3D printing market will surpass $9.5 billion by 2032. It is most commonly used within orthodontics and prosthodontics; however, use cases are popping up in every specialty as the months progress. The advantages of 3D printing are not just limited to speed—3D printing is allowing for greater customisation and precision at a lower cost than traditional milling methods. Clinics that incorporate in-house 3D printers are finding they can control quality more tightly. They are finding patients appreciate a faster service (often same-day service!), and reduce reliance on third-party labs. 2. AI-Powered Treatment Planning AI is becoming a valuable aid for clinicians in 2025. It is no longer limited to diagnostics — it’s now playing an active role in how we plan treatment. There’s a big reason why it’s one of the hottest dental trends this year. Platforms using artificial intelligence can now analyse patient data, radiographs, and scans to recommend treatment plans. Integrations between software and scanners are rapidly improving. You can combine multiple tools to flag potential issues, and optimise workflows. One example: some orthodontic AI systems such as SoftSmile can simulate tooth movement in seconds, helping both patients and clinicians visualise outcomes before treatment even begins. However, it’s important to understand that AI cannot replace clinical judgment. Nor should it ever aim to do so. AI allows clinicians to make more informed decisions, faster—and with greater accuracy. With growing demand for dentistry globally, clinicians will be required to see a higher number of patients in a shorter amount of time. AI tools enable you to do this without compromising on your standard of care. 3. Teledentistry Since the pandemic, teledentistry has matured into a legitimate tool for triage, follow-ups and consultations. In 2024, the ADA reported that 1 in 5 dental patients had used some form of virtual consultation, and that number is climbing. It is increasingly convenient for patients to address minor issues through a video or telephone call. In fact, many orthodontists are using remote monitoring software to complement teledentistry solutions to reduce the number of in-person reviews. There are advantages for both parties involved. For patients, it’s about convenience and access. For practices, it’s a way to increase efficiency, and optimise chair time. It is particularly important for domiciliary patients, or patients with limited mobility to access dental care. And as licensure and insurance barriers continue to adapt, more clinics are integrating teledentistry into their long-term patient experience strategy. 4. Laser Dentistry Laser technology isn’t new, but it’s developing into a mature technology that is trending in 2025. More general practices are investing in soft tissue and hard tissue lasers as a way to offer less invasive procedures with faster healing times. It is particularly useful in cosmetic cases, where soft tissue surgery needs to incur less inflammation in visible areas. Even with routine procedures such as cavity preparation, lasers can reduce bleeding at the gingival margin, and often eliminate the need for anaesthesia in smaller procedures. This is a massive draw for new patients who seek more pain-free alternatives, and don’t want to undergo sedation. The barrier to entry has dropped too. Devices are more affordable, and training is more accessible than ever. For many practices, adopting laser technology is a no-brainer for providing optimal care. 5. Customized Clear Aligners, Prosthetics and Implants Personalisation is almost becoming a buzzword in dentistry. And, clear aligner technology is leading the way. Clinics can now offer fully custom aligner systems tailored to each patient’s anatomy, treatment goals, and preferences. They are less reliant on third-party brands, dictating the patterns of movement. This has ultimately improved the experience for both clinicians and patients – with less refinements, more predictable outcomes, and cheaper treatment. However, this trend doesn’t stop at orthodontics. Prosthetics, surgical guides, and implant abutments are now routinely customised by the clinicians. What used to require third-party manufacturers and long wait times can now be delivered in-house or through advanced cloud-based platforms. This is improving access to many patients – which can only be a net positive for dentistry as a a whole.



In 2025, the idea of offering generic treatment modalities are out of the question. The more personalised your offering, the more attractive it is. Dental Patient Trends The patient journey is integral to the growth of a dental clinic. Many doctors make the mistake of restricting their perception of the patient journey to the clinical aspect. But in 2025, the benchmark of a good patient experience is only escalating further. Engagement is no longer just about sending appointment reminders or a quick post-op check-in. It’s about building long-term trust. It’s about providing simple communication that patients can refer back to. Here are six trends that reflect how clinics are stepping up their game. 1. Digital Patient Engagement Patients expect to interact with healthcare providers the same way they do with banks or airlines—digitally, and on their own terms. Dental clinics are finally catching up to this expectation. The traditional model of ringing a busy phone line to queue up for an appointment is outdated. Automated reminders and text updates are quickly becoming the norm for many clinics. What’s interesting is how much this affects perception. A recent study by Accenture showed that 70% of patients say a provider’s digital capabilities influence their loyalty. This isn’t simply limited to large DSOs—small clinics are increasingly using digital tools to create smoother onboarding, fewer phone calls, and more streamlined follow-ups. The technology is more accessible than ever – and many of the newer practice management software are integrating this within their back end. Clinics that embrace this are seeing fewer no-shows, better compliance, and higher satisfaction scores—all without needing to grow their admin teams. 2. Personalized Treatment Plans Patients hate feeling pushed into treatment. Ultimately, they want options that make sense for them. That’s where personalised treatment planning has made a difference. Practices can now use a combination of AI diagnostic software, and chairside communication tools such as Chairsyde and Diagnocat to communicate their treatment plans. Patients feel seen. And when patients feel seen, they’re far more likely to say yes to treatment. You don’t need to reinvent your entire workflow to do this. Even subtle shifts—like presenting multiple pathways with pros and cons, or filming a short video—can create a deeper sense of involvement. In a world where comparison shopping is the norm, personalization is one of the strongest differentiators a clinic can offer. 3. Patient Support Chatbots No one likes waiting on hold. And in 2025, they shouldn’t have to. AI-powered chatbots can prevent you losing out on leads – regardless of the time of day. Many of them can be trusted to handle the basics: FAQs, appointment requests, pre-screening, and even insurance queries. Used properly, chatbots don’t replace human contact. Instead, they can act more like a filter for more intricate enquiries. This frees up capacity for your front desk to focus on building patient rapport, and addressing bigger concerns. The real power here is triage. Many systems can now escalate complex queries to a live team member while handling everything else automatically. It’s a smoother experience for everyone involved, and it’s especially useful after hours when traditional support isn’t available. 4. Use of AR and VR (to Reduce Anxiety) Dental anxiety is one of the most common barriers to treatment—and we’re finally getting better at addressing it. In 2025, clinics are turning to augmented and virtual reality to help patients feel more in control. VR headsets can now immerse patients in calming environments during procedures. This is currently being tested within a number of pediatric dental clinics across the US, whereby clinicians can project animated films or visual cues to calm patients. On the other hand, AR tools are also being used to visually explain treatment outcomes. For example, some orthodontic practices use AR to project a simulation of a patient’s future smile. It is far easier for patients to visualise their desired result when it is superimposed on their own face! These tools are no longer experimental. The cost of VR headsets are beginning to drop as more competitors enter the market. They're becoming part of standard anxiety management, especially among younger patients who are already used to immersive tech. 5. Patient Retention and Loyalty Programs Attracting new patients is expensive. The cost of paid ads are rising. The effectiveness of social media is waning. This is why many clinics are pivoting their focus onto patient retention. All things considered, it is more cost-effective. That’s why 2025 has seen a rise in loyalty programs that reward long-term engagement—not just treatment completion. Think beyond the traditional “refer a friend” model. Practices are now offering exclusive member benefits, annual care packages, discounts on cosmetic treatments, or priority booking for routine care. The goal is to make patients feel like part of something—not just a number in the system. And it works. Clinics that run structured retention programs often report increases for annual examination attendance, especially among fee-for-service patients. When patients feel appreciated, they stay. And when they stay, they refer. 6. Sustainable Dental Products Sustainability has moved from niche concern to mainstream expectation. Patients are asking more questions about where their products come from, and how they’re disposed of. The onus is now on the clinician to ensure they are sourcing their products from sustainable sources. Biodegradable toothbrushes, recyclable aligner packaging, refillable oral care kits — these are no longer fringe ideas. They’re becoming standard in forward-thinking practices. Even things like digital scanners (vs traditional PVS) are seen as eco-friendlier alternatives beyond the obvious clinical advantages. For younger patients especially, sustainability is often tied directly to brand loyalty. By aligning your practice with environmentally responsible choices, you're not only helping the planet. You’re also appealing to a patient base that values conscious decision-making. These trends reflect a wider shift happening in the dental world. It is no longer an authoritative profession, whereby the dentist dictates the entire patient journey.



It’s no longer just about clinical outcomes—it’s about how patients feel throughout their journey. And in 2025, that experience is largely shaped by how well your practice listens, adapts, and communicates. Dental Workforce and Practices Trends Technology isn’t the only thing changing in dentistry. Behind the scenes, structural shifts are reshaping how practices operate. The ownership models are changing from DSOs to smaller corporates. Independent practices are seeking more efficiency to free up chair time. From workforce challenges to new business models, clinics are navigating more complexity than ever. Those who adapt quickly are reaping the rewards. Here are four trends redefining the business of dentistry in 2025: 1. Addressing Staffing Shortages at Dental Practices Workforce shortages remain one of the most pressing challenges across dentistry worldwide. Recruitment is increasingly competitive. Hygienists, dental assistants and treatment coordinators are still in high demand. Amongst all of those professionals, dentists are still in significant demand. In 2024, the ADA reported that more than 35% of dental practices were actively hiring, yet struggling to fill roles. The reasons are suspected to be multifactorial: burnout, early retirement post-COVID, shifting generational expectations, and limited training pipelines. In many sectors, the part-time or hybrid model is becoming popularised. Obviously, dentistry doesn’t cater to the hybrid model; however, workers are increasingly favouring part-time work to foster a better work-life balance. In response, clinics are rethinking everything from compensation packages to culture. Many are offering upskilling opportunities (by way of CPD/CE courses or postgraduate training), flexible scheduling, and clear growth pathways to retain talent. Others are investing in automation and AI to reduce pressure on overstretched staff. The key is to implement these changes with minimal impact on the patient experience. The last thing you want is to be more efficient, but ultimately less profitable in the long term. 2. The Rise of Dental Support Organizations Dental Support Organizations (DSOs) continue to reshape how practices grow and survive. These groups provide non-clinical support to affiliated practices, covering everything from HR and payroll to marketing, compliance, and procurement. For clinicians, this can allow more focus on what they enjoy through their clinical role. In 2025, DSOs aren’t just expanding – they’re being forced to evolve. Smaller, specialty-specific DSOs are emerging alongside the big players. Offering niche services is proving to be a profitable model, versus the traditional large group practices. Some even allow partial autonomy, giving owners more flexibility while still accessing group-level infrastructure. For new grads, DSOs can offer a soft landing with mentorship and reduced overhead risk. For established owners, they’re a pathway to scale without selling out completely. This model isn’t for everyone—but for many, it’s becoming hard to ignore. 3. Digitalizing Workflow with Practice Management Software The era of paper charts is becoming quickly outdated. With increased regulation through HIPAA/GDPR compliance, digital workflows are far more advantageous. You may think this is a change that occurred in the last decade. However, digital practice management extends way beyond organising a clinical diary. Modern PMS platforms now integrate everything—scheduling, treatment planning, billing, imaging, communication, even analytics. The best systems help to track KPIs in real time, which can be a massive help to independent practice owners. Convenience is one of the more minor advantages when it comes to digitising your workflow. When your front desk, clinicians, and treatment coordinators are using the same workflow, things move faster and cleaner. Errors begin to be eliminated. Patient experience improves. What’s changed in the last year is the level of integration. Many systems now connect with AI diagnostic tools, patient engagement platforms, and inventory management—all in one dashboard. The daily workflow substantially improves for everyone involved. 4. Dental Group Practices Independent practices are thriving, but group practices are rapidly growing. With the rising costs of overheads, it is becoming increasingly difficult for single-handed practice owners to manage. This shift isn’t just about size. It’s about resilience to cope with these overheads. Group setups can share overheads, pool specialist expertise, and offer a wider range of services under one roof. For patients, this often means better continuity of care. For clinicians, it’s a way to offload business pressures. Ultimately, having multiple skilled clinicians in one building increases the opportunity for cross-specialty collaboration. This prevents the outflow of patients to other practices. In many cases, groups are hybrid: a mix of owner-dentists, associates, and specialists working under one shared brand or building. And because they often run on unified systems, decision-making becomes more strategic and scalable. There’s also the factor of leverage to consider. Group practices are better positioned to negotiate with suppliers, navigate compliance, and adapt to economic fluctuations—something solo owners are finding increasingly difficult to manage alone. As the dental landscape becomes more complex, so does the business of running a practice.

Sustainable growth is only possible for clinicians that embrace flexibility and adaptability. Smarter team structures will allow clinics to grow more efficiently, and result in the best outcomes of survival long term.
